messages.content:
## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Python program: pass one whole, legal
Python program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is executed exactly as you wrote it, as the whole of a `program.py`
with `__name__` set to `"__main__"`.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg.session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg.docs`: Find what the agent can call, and take a documentation view back out of the window. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.files`: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.views`: Show a file, a computed value, or an entry's documentation. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.session`: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this agent's role. — brought into scope with `import gg`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window
- `Documentation` — documentation or a skill you asked to read, delivered on the following turn
- `File` — a file, or a window of one, shown in your context — seeded by the run or opened by your own file-view call — headed by its path, the 1-based line range shown and the file's total line count, as `File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines` (a whole file's range runs `1-N`)
- `View` — a value your program put into your window; the view's label follows the heading, as `View: changed-files`

For example, lines 100 to 250 of a 400-line file you opened a view of arrive
as:

```
File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines
----
...those lines of the file...
```

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

Task
----
Create the file `notes/plan.md` in the workspace. Its required content is specified in `specs/plan-brief.md`, which is already open in your context. Write the file exactly as the brief specifies.

Documentation: gg.docs.search
----
search(*, query: str | None = None, modules: list[str] | None = None, type: str | None = None, kind: DocKind | None = None, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> DocSearch
  query?: str | None = None (passed by name) — The words to match, as a case-insensitive substring. The default is no query at all, which is what turns a filter into a directory rather than a search.
  modules?: list[str] | None = None (passed by name) — The modules to look in, each named by its gg id — `files`, `views`, `docs` — or by the path a program imports it under — `gg.files` — and matched exactly. Several name a union: an entry in any one of them is a hit, so one call lists a whole granted surface. With no `query` it is those modules' whole directory. A name no module has matches nothing rather than failing, so an empty page means the filter found nothing, not that it was rejected. The default is no module filter at all.
  type?: str | None = None (passed by name) — One type's name, narrowing to that type and to the functions that take or return it. Like `modules`, a name nothing declares matches nothing rather than failing.
  kind?: DocKind | None = None (passed by name) — Whether to return modules, functions or types. The default returns all three.
  offset?: int | None = None (passed by name) — How many hits to skip, for reading past the first page. The default starts at the best hit.
  limit?: int | None = None (passed by name) — The most hits to return. The default is gg's own page size and there is a ceiling above it, so comparing `len(hits)` against `total` is the only way to see a capped page. Zero is refused rather than read as "no cap".

Defined in `gg.docs`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Search every module, function and type the agent can call, by keyword and by filter.

This is how a name is found. Matching is a case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `open_docs_view`. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched — an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph — and a weaker kind never overtakes a stronger one however often it occurs.

Only entries this run bound are returned, so nothing a search finds is something the run withheld. Every argument is optional and they compose with each other: a query alone ranks the whole surface, a filter alone is a directory of what it names, and the two together search inside the filter.

The page comes back as a value and is also opened as a view, under the selector `search results`, so it can be read on the next turn without a program showing it to itself. The next search replaces that view: it names what is being worked from rather than keeping a record.

Returns: The page that matched, best first. `total` counts every entry that matched before paging, so a page shorter than `total` is a page there is more of.

Raises `ApiError`: `invalid-argument` for a call with no query and no filter at all — nothing matched and nothing was asked for are different answers — and for a `limit` of zero, which would ask for a page that answers nothing. A `modules` entry or a `type` that names something gg does not hold is not among them: it matches nothing.

Documentation: gg.core.ApiError
----
class ApiError(Exception):
    operation: str
    code: ApiErrorCode

Defined in `gg.core`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

A gg call that failed.

WIT models a failure as `result<T, api-error>`, and a surface that handed that back as a pair would force a branch after every line. Python's own answer is an exception, so that is what this SDK raises: the happy path is already unwrapped, and a failure that nobody expected ends the program with gg told which call failed and on which line.

A failure that is expected is an ordinary `except` on `code`:

```python
import gg

try:
    gg.views.open_text("build log", log)
except gg.core.ApiError as failure:
    if failure.code is not gg.core.ApiErrorCode.LIMIT_EXCEEDED:
        raise
    gg.views.open_text("build log (tail)", log[-40_000:])
```
  operation: str — The gg call that failed, under gg's own name for it (`read_file`, `spawn_subagent`).

It is gg's name for the capability rather than this SDK's spelling of it, so it is the same word in every language a program may be written in.
  code: ApiErrorCode — The failure class, so a handler branches on a value rather than on prose.

Documentation: gg.views.open_file
----
open_file(path: str, *, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None, max_line_chars: int | None = None) -> FileRead
  path: str — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: int | None = None (passed by name) — The 1-based line to start at.
  limit?: int | None = None (passed by name) — How many lines to show from `offset`.
  max_line_chars?: int | None = None (passed by name) — The most characters of each line to show, 1 to 65,536; a longer line is cut there and annotated with how many characters were dropped. The default shows lines whole.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

The split from `files.read_file` is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

The view's text body is held to the same 65,536-byte cap an `open_text` body is: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened — never a truncation. The way out is a narrower window, with `offset` and `limit`, or `max_line_chars`, which cuts each line of the view longer than that many characters at that point and annotates it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, with the count of characters dropped. The cut is the view's alone — what this call returns and the file itself are untouched — and the byte cap is measured against the body after it, which is what lets a window over a log of enormous lines fit. Left out, lines arrive whole. A picture is not a text body and is not subject to the cap.

Returns: Exactly what `files.read_file` hands back for the same file, so the program holds the contents as well as the model holding the view.

Raises `ApiError`: `not-found` for a missing path, `invalid-argument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `max_line_chars` of zero or over 65,536, and `limit-exceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text window over the cap. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.

Documentation: gg.files.FileRead
----
FileRead = TextFile | ImageFile

Defined in `gg.files`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

What a read returned: a text file's window, or a picture's description.

A picture is a different kind of thing from text, so it is a different class rather than a string that happens to be binary. `isinstance(read, TextFile)`, or a `match` on the two, is what narrows it, and a program that treats an image as text is caught by that check instead of silently writing an empty string somewhere.

Search every module, function and type the agent can call, by keyword and by filter.

This is how a name is found. Matching is a case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `open_docs_view`. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched — an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph — and a weaker kind never overtakes a stronger one however often it occurs.

Only entries this run bound are returned, so nothing a search finds is something the run withheld. Every argument is optional and they compose with each other: a query alone ranks the whole surface, a filter alone is a directory of what it names, and the two together search inside the filter.

The page comes back as a value and is also opened as a view, under the selector `search results`, so it can be read on the next turn without a program showing it to itself. The next search replaces that view: it names what is being worked from rather than keeping a record.

class ApiError(Exception):
    operation: str
    code: ApiErrorCode

Defined in `gg.core`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

A gg call that failed.

WIT models a failure as `result<T, api-error>`, and a surface that handed that back as a pair would force a branch after every line. Python's own answer is an exception, so that is what this SDK raises: the happy path is already unwrapped, and a failure that nobody expected ends the program with gg told which call failed and on which line.

A failure that is expected is an ordinary `except` on `code`:

```python
try:
    gg.views.open_text("build log", log)
except gg.core.ApiError as failure:
    if failure.code is not gg.core.ApiErrorCode.LIMIT_EXCEEDED:
        raise
    gg.views.open_text("build log (tail)", log[-40_000:])
```

It is gg's name for the capability rather than this SDK's spelling of it, so it is the same word in every language a program may be written in.
  code: ApiErrorCode — The failure class, so a handler branches on a value rather than on prose.

Only entries this run bound are returned, so nothing a search finds is something the run withheld. Every argument is optional and they compose with each other: a query alone ranks the whole surface, a filter alone is a directory of what it names, and the two together search inside the filter.

The page comes back as a value and is also opened as a view, under the selector `search results`, so it can be read on the next turn without a program showing it to itself. The next search replaces that view: it names what is being worked from rather than keeping a record.

Returns: The page that matched, best first. `total` counts every entry that matched before paging, so a page shorter than `total` is a page there is more of.

Raises `ApiError`: `invalid-argument` for a call with no query and no filter at all — nothing matched and nothing was asked for are different answers — and for a `limit` of zero, which would ask for a page that answers nothing. A `modules` entry or a `type` that names something gg does not hold is not among them: it matches nothing.

class ApiError(Exception):
    operation: str
    code: ApiErrorCode

Defined in `gg.core`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

A gg call that failed.

WIT models a failure as `result<T, api-error>`, and a surface that handed that back as a pair would force a branch after every line. Python's own answer is an exception, so that is what this SDK raises: the happy path is already unwrapped, and a failure that nobody expected ends the program with gg told which call failed and on which line.

A failure that is expected is an ordinary `except` on `code`:

```python
import gg

try:
    gg.views.open_text("build log", log)
except gg.core.ApiError as failure:
    if failure.code is not gg.core.ApiErrorCode.LIMIT_EXCEEDED:
        raise
    gg.views.open_text("build log (tail)", log[-40_000:])
```

It is gg's name for the capability rather than this SDK's spelling of it, so it is the same word in every language a program may be written in.

open_file(path: str, *, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None, max_line_chars: int | None = None) -> FileRead
  path: str — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: int | None = None (passed by name) — The 1-based line to start at.
  limit?: int | None = None (passed by name) — How many lines to show from `offset`.
  max_line_chars?: int | None = None (passed by name) — The most characters of each line to show, 1 to 65,536; a longer line is cut there and annotated with how many characters were dropped. The default shows lines whole.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

The split from `files.read_file` is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

The view's text body is held to the same 65,536-byte cap an `open_text` body is: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened — never a truncation. The way out is a narrower window, with `offset` and `limit`, or `max_line_chars`, which cuts each line of the view longer than that many characters at that point and annotates it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, with the count of characters dropped. The cut is the view's alone — what this call returns and the file itself are untouched — and the byte cap is measured against the body after it, which is what lets a window over a log of enormous lines fit. Left out, lines arrive whole. A picture is not a text body and is not subject to the cap.

Returns: Exactly what `files.read_file` hands back for the same file, so the program holds the contents as well as the model holding the view.

Raises `ApiError`: `not-found` for a missing path, `invalid-argument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `max_line_chars` of zero or over 65,536, and `limit-exceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text window over the cap. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.
